analysis.one_liner: Bans debt collectors from trying to collect debts whose legal time limit has expired.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee in November 2019 and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Some collectors sue or harass people over very old debts even after the legal window for enforcing them has closed. Today, collectors can often threaten a lawsuit to scare someone into paying, and making any payment can restart the clock on a debt courts can no longer enforce. This bill would amend the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act to make it illegal for a debt collector to collect or attempt to collect any debt on which the statute of limitations has expired.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who are contacted about old, legally unenforceable debts. They would no longer face threats of lawsuits over time-barred debt, and a payment or acknowledgment of the debt could not be used to revive a lawsuit against them.

how_it_helps.text: Adds a new section 811A to the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act stating that a debt collector may not collect, or attempt to collect, any consumer debt on which the statute of limitations has expired.
Because it amends the FDP Act, violations would fall under that law's existing enforcement framework, which lets consumers sue collectors who break the rules.

analysis.who_pays: Debt buyers and collection agencies that profit from acquiring and pursuing charged-off debts, including time-barred ones. Their ability to pressure consumers into paying debts courts can no longer enforce would end.

drawbacks.text: Some consumers do owe these old debts, and a ban means creditors and collectors can never recover those amounts, which can be priced into the cost of credit offered to everyone.

Critics of similar restrictions have argued that collectors should be allowed to ask for voluntary repayment of valid debts even when a court can no longer force payment; the bill takes away that option entirely.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection is real and targeted: courts in many states already refuse to enforce time-barred debts, so the bill mostly stops collectors from doing through threats and pressure what courts will not do. The cost falls on the debt-buying industry, though a share of the loss could show up in slightly tighter credit for subprime borrowers. On balance, a straightforward consumer protection with a narrow, honest trade-off.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Financial Services Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen introduced the bill on November 12, 2019, with seven original cosponsors.
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services, and no further action appears in its history — no hearing, no markup, no vote.
It attracted 11 Democratic cosponsors over its lifetime and none from the Republican side.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill was not reintroduced in the record provided.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Debt buyers and collection agencies are better off: they keep the ability to pursue time-barred debts by phone, letter, and lawsuit threats, and no one else gained anything because the bill never even reached a debate.

for.name: Rep. Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited seven original cosponsors.

for.name: 11 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Maxine Waters (D-CA)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral: no hearing, no markup, no vote was ever scheduled for the bill.

against.name: Debt collection industry
against.what_they_did: The industry has long opposed bans on collecting time-barred debt, which make up a meaningful share of the charged-off debt it buys and pursues.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and none were Republicans, but the bill never got a hearing or a vote, so the chamber's actual party split was never tested.

industries.note: Time-barred debt is a significant slice of the charged-off debt this industry buys cheaply and pursues; the bill would end its ability to collect or threaten litigation on those debts. The industry's gain comes directly out of consumers' pockets, often from people pressured into paying debts they no longer legally owe.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and consumer lenders
industries.note: Lenders could no longer recover old unpaid balances through collectors, which they may offset by pricing risk into credit. The immediate effect on most lenders, though, is small compared with the effect on collectors.
